Escalator

One chain, two wheel tracks: how every step stays level on the slope.

An escalator is a staircase that never stops. Every step rides an endless loop: up the slope, round the top, and back underneath. This one rises three metres at thirty degrees, and every tread stays level all the way up. So how does a step stay flat on a slope?

Behind the figure

An escalator is a staircase that never stops: 53 steps ride one endless loop, up the slope, round the top and back underneath. This one rises 3000 mm at 30° and runs at 0.5 m/s.

How it is computed

  • The chain path is lines and arcs, with 53 steps at 400 mm along it.
  • Each step is a rigid body. The trailer-wheel track is the path the trailer wheel traces while the tread is held level; it is computed, not drawn by hand.
  • Tests sweep the chain through a whole pitch, 5 mm at a time, for both inclines. They check that no two steps touch, that each wheel stays on its own rail, that every tread is level within 0.5° on the slope, and that the treads are flat at the landings.
  • Step width 1000 mm (not drawn). Dimensions in mm.
